nameStory: Forster's Tern gets its name from Johann Reinhold Forster, a German naturalist who sailed with Captain Cook on his second voyage around the world in the 1770s. While Forster never visited New England, his contributions to natural history were so significant that this graceful marsh-dwelling tern bears his name. The word 'tern' itself comes from the Old English 'stearn,' reflecting these birds' ancient presence in human awareness.
description: Forster's Tern is a medium-sized seabird with the classic tern look: sleek and elegant with long, pointed wings built for diving. These graceful birds measure about 13-14 inches long with a wingspan of roughly 2.5 feet, making them slightly smaller than a crow but with much more slender proportions. They sport pale gray backs, bright white undersides, and distinctive red-orange bills tipped with black during breeding season. Unlike many terns that prefer coastal waters, Forster's Terns are marsh specialists, making their living in inland wetlands and salt marshes.

idTips.label: Winter Eye Mask
idTips.description: In fall and winter, look for the distinctive black comma-shaped mark that curves around and behind each eye, contrasting sharply with the otherwise white head - this is the field mark that instantly separates Forster's from Common Terns

idTips.label: Tail Pattern
idTips.description: The white tail has gray outer edges (rather than dark outer edges), creating a subtle but distinctive pattern visible when the bird banks or hovers

idTips.label: Bill Color
idTips.description: During breeding season, the bill glows bright red-orange with a crisp black tip, like it's been dipped in ink - in winter it becomes mostly dark

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: The upperwings appear notably pale and uniform gray without the darker 'wedge' of black wingtips that Common Terns display

idTips.label: Voice
idTips.description: Gives typical tern calls but also produces harsher, more gull-like sounds that can remind you of a small Bonaparte's Gull

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Almost always found around marshes and wetlands rather than open ocean, often seen diving in shallow brackish water or cattail-bordered ponds

habitat: In New England, Forster's Terns favor salt marshes, brackish ponds, and coastal wetlands with emergent vegetation like cattails and sedges. They're particularly drawn to areas where fresh and salt water mix, such as the extensive marshlands around Cape Cod, the Connecticut River delta, and similar wetland complexes along the coast. Unlike their Common Tern cousins who prefer open beaches, Forster's Terns need the sheltered, vegetation-rich environment that marshes provide.

seasonality.spring: Arriving migrants appear in April and May, often still showing winter plumage with the characteristic black eye masks before transitioning to breeding colors with bright red bills.
seasonality.summer: Peak breeding season when birds display full breeding plumage with bright red-orange bills and may be seen carrying fish to feed mates and young in marsh colonies.
seasonality.fall: Migration peaks in August and September as birds molt back to winter plumage, making the black eye mask the key identification feature as breeding colors fade.
seasonality.winter: Most have departed for southern wintering grounds, though occasional individuals may linger into early winter in milder coastal areas, always showing the distinctive black eye comma.

funFact: Forster's Terns are one of the few tern species that actually become easier to identify in winter - while most birds become more confusing in their drab winter plumage, the Forster's Tern develops its most distinctive field mark, that unmistakable black eye mask that no other tern in New England wears.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Common Tern, especially during breeding season when both have red bills and gray-and-white plumage. Remember the simple rule: 'Forster's winter face is fancy' - the black eye mask in fall and winter is diagnostic. In breeding plumage, look for Forster's paler, more uniform wing color and gray-edged (not dark-edged) tail.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being named for a European naturalist, Forster's Tern is a distinctly North American species that's quite rare in Europe. The few that show up across the Atlantic are considered exciting vagrants by European birders - a reminder of how bird migration can sometimes take individuals far from their normal range.
compareHints: Forster's Tern differs from Common Tern most obviously in winter with its black eye mask versus the Common's black cap extending to the eye. Arctic Terns are extremely rare in New England and have shorter red bills and legs. Roseate Terns are whiter overall with much longer tail streamers and black bills during breeding season, plus they prefer rocky coastal islands rather than marshes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to other New England terns, Common Terns are the most likely to be seen inland on lakes and rivers, while Roseate Terns stick closer to saltwater and have longer, more deeply forked tails.
Compared to Common Terns, Roseates are more delicate with longer, more elegant proportions and that distinctive pink breast wash.
Among New England's terns, Arctic Terns are distinguished from Common Terns by their solid red bills (no black tip) and more deeply forked tails.
